surfaces.part: snow cap on top of rock

answer.evidence: The silhouette is a rounded mound that widens from 3 px at row 3 to 13 px at rows 8-9, then narrows to 2 px at row 14. White snow covers the upper rows (about 4-8) as a lit top surface. It ends where the grey mid-tone rock begins (x=8 changes from white to L=125 grey at row 8, x=11 from white to grey at row 8). Below it, rows 9-14 hold a darker grey front face that gets darker toward the base (L=98, 126, 79). The edge between snow and rock is a loose, irregular organic transition, not a clean edge line, so this is a moderate-confidence call. Overall it reads as a snow-topped rock seen from above and in front, not a flat elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tiny snow rock, under one tile (about 10x10 source px), set against two full-size leafy trees. The kind match is loose because a rock is not a plant. Its 13 colours give only about 4 grey-white steps, against 6-7 or more on the trees. The measured facts show 100% near-neutral dark edge pixels, and the picture agrees: a grey-black outline wraps the whole blob with no tint, which is the sticker look. The references show 0% neutral, with dark green and brown tones next to the leaves and wood. A small dot or two of shading on the stone is not the per-stone facet shading and grain a careful artist would put beside the reference. Because the piece is under one tile, the per-tile density facts do not count against it. By eye it still looks flatter and thinner than the reference, and when in doubt the rule is to fail.
